body:
I've started using the annotation in my project and finding bugs to fix. Most importantly, the write-to-override features does not seem to work. Looking at the code, it should never have worked. And yet I recall testing it and having it work 😅 I would not have made the PR if I'd realized such a big part of was faulty.

Having said this, however, I am considering cutting it altogether since I am trying to pinpoint the mechanics of this feature.
The core components of it are:
1. Theming a property makes it so the engine updates it when appropriate
2. Theming a property surfaces the corresponding theme override in the editor

This leaves us to decide what happens exactly when the user tries to set it. Turning writes into overrides has some pros and cons::
- Pro: gives a string-less way to set overrides
- Pro: gives the user a way to set the themed property without getting confused as to why the set value "changes by itself" later.
- Con: the mechanism is implicit
- Con: makes the usage of setters impossible

This last con is what is giving me some thoughts. When using the feature in my project, I've realized that about half of the time I use `get_theme_*`, I am doing some extra processing with the fetched values. Often, custom controls have children, and theme items set in the root control's theme type need to be passed down to the children via theme overrides. Sometimes, the value in the theme is just a base value that needs to be multiplied or changed in some way. One can do these operations in `_notification()` but I feel like they would also naturally fit in the property's own setter/getter.

Setters wouldn't work well with the write-to-override mechanic, but I think they might be more useful overall, so one or the other must be chosen. In the end, I think it might be worthwhile to scale back on the complexity of the semantics of the feature. Maybe themed properties don't need a special write behavior, whether it be write-to-override or read-only. Maybe it's just fine if they are properties that get their value set by the engine at specific times, and the user can do whatever operation they need with them with that understanding. Although in that case there should certainly be a warning if the user tries to write to a themed property outside of a setter, just to gently remind them that whatever value they write is most likely going to be overwritten, and if they know what they're doing they can just silence it.

I agree that themed properties don't need setters. None of the built-in ones have setter, they are always either set in theme or via override.

That said, I'd expect the property to be equivalent of using `get_theme_something()` method. Right now it only reads the override, which is not very useful. Though looking at the docs, it seems to be a bug.

Another thing I noticed is that the custom classes with themed properties are not selectable in Theme editor. But that's not easy to fix.

Why `@themed` is vararg? The `args` is never explained.

> That said, I'd expect the property to be equivalent of using `get_theme_something()` method. Right now it only reads the override, which is not very useful. Though looking at the docs, it seems to be a bug.

You've probably not set the correct theme type variation? As mentioned in the OP, due to the way the theme type tree is traversed (theme variation tree traversed if present, then native class tree until Control/Window is reached, no script classes ever considered in the process) you still need to assign a properly set up theme type variation with a matching name to the class_name. As I stated in the OP this is far from ideal and I must create a second PR adding the necessary extra behavior. I've just been busy with work and my own personal projects.

But if you do that, it _should_ work. I use this feature to handle everything about theme in my personal project using a self-compiled version of Godot and it works. If you're doing that already and it still doesn't work, then it's a a bug and I'll need some reproduction steps.

> Another thing I noticed is that the custom classes with themed properties are not selectable in Theme editor. But that's not easy to fix.

Since the custom theme types are registered with the ThemeDB, I assume the theme editor hasn't been update to query the ThemeDB rather than the theme defaults file. I did not touch anything regarding the user interface, so I can't be sure. I'll look into it.

> Why `@themed` is vararg? The `args` is never explained.

By examining the signature of other annotations, I developed the impression an annotation definition had to be vararg in order to have default arguments. If that's not the case, then I misunderstood.

> You've probably not set the correct theme type variation?

This should be mentioned in the doc.

> By examining the signature of other annotations, I developed the impression an annotation definition had to be vararg in order to have default arguments.

`@export_custom` has default argument and isn't vararg.
This work looked so promossing, but seams to have halted. This seams to be needed.
